{"type":"tool_call_update","toolCallId":"call-4194e39d-da65-4a1f-a3c0-277a49735197-2","status":"in_progress","content":[{"type":"content","content":{"type":"text","text":" same shelf sized for the wide bin: three columns instead of two.\"\n\n[variants.shelf_gridfinity_3x2.params]\ngrid_x = 3\nbracket_count = 6\n\n[variants.shelf_gridfinity_3x2.accepted]\nsliver = 26\n```\n\nThe test is whether it is the same geometry. A wider cradle on the same J is a variant.\nA different mechanism is a part, however similar the slab looks.\n\n`note` is one sentence saying why the variant exists, written in the user's words rather than the doctrine's, because the viewer shows it next to the variant and its reader is whoever is about to print the thing. The params are the how and never the why: `diagonal = true` explains nothing to someone who has not read the doctrine, and \"prints tilted so it needs no supports\" does.\n\n## Measurements\n\nThe bottleneck on a one-off is not geometry, it is dimensions. A wrong number produces a\nperfect model of the wrong object, and nothing downstream can catch it.\n\n**Ask for a measurement. Never improvise one.** A guessed clearance that happens to\nbuild is worse than a failure, because it prints. Record what you are told in\n`measurements.toml` at the project root, with how it was obtained, and read it with\n`measured()`:\n\n```toml\n[shelf_depth]\nvalue = 340\nunit = \"mm\"\nhow = \"tape measure, freezer middle shelf, 2026-07-20\"\n```\n\n```python\nfrom nurb import measured\n\ndepth = measured(\"shelf_depth\")\n```\n\nAn unknown name raises, naming what is on file. That failure is the point: it is the\nmoment to ask rather than to pick something plausible.\n\n**A published number is a measurement, not a guess.** When the part mates with a manufactured product or a published standard, a VESA mount, a gridfinity bin, a camera thread, the number already exists in a datasheet, and making somebody caliper a hole pattern a standards body fixed is friction wearing rigor's clothes. Research it, record it like any other measurement with `how` naming the source (\"VESA MIS-D 100, manufacturer product page\"), and ask only for what nobody published, like the opening the finished thing has to fit. Two limits keep this honest: the user's actual object outranks the spec when the two disagree, because clones drift, and a number inferred from a product photo or a listing's marketing copy was never published at all, so it is a guess and gets marked like one.\n\n**A photo is a shape, never a dimension.** It can identify the standard, that the siding is dutch lap, that the rail is 2020 extrusion, and the published profile carries the numbers from there. Pixels carry no millimetres, so a dimension read off a photo is a guess and gets marked like one.\n\n**A phone scan is reference geometry, not metrology.** Its error changes with the phone, capture mode, surface and technique, so no universal millimetre threshold makes it a caliper. `nurb scan` reads the mesh in mm, states the units it used, and slices profile polylines to sketch against. Record what it gave with `how` naming the file and the slice, and keep every scan-derived fit `provisional` until a coupon proves it against the real object.\n\n**A fit coupon turns a loose measurement into a tight one.** Before printing a part modelled against a scan or a photo, print the mating surface alone: a thin strip carrying just the profile, minutes of filament. Held against the real object it shows every gap the numbers hid, the parameters get corrected, and only then does the full part print. A coupon that fits is what takes the provisional flag off.\n\n**When there is nobody to ask**, write the guess down and mark it `provisional = true`.\nThe danger was never the guess, it is that a guess and a measurement look identical six\nmonths later. `how` is still required, because \"eyeballed against a broom\" tells the\nnext person how far to trust it, and `nurb check` lists every provisional value until\nsomebody picks up a caliper.\n\nA measured value pays for itself across a family. Notch measured one bracket pitch and\namortized it over sixteen parts.\n\n## Assemblies\n\nEvery rule above judges one solid being manufactured. An assembly judges solids being\nused together: a door on its mount, a lid over the machine it covers. The failure it\nexists for built clean, checked clean, exported watertight and printed beautifully,\nthen jammed at 45 degrees of its swing, because the collision between two correct\nparts existed only in the physical world. No per-solid rule can have an opinion about\nmotion.\n\nThe contract mirrors a part's. An assembly is a function in `parts/` whose keyword\ndefaults are its parameters; what it returns is placed solids rather than one solid.\n`use(name)` builds a sibling part where it was modelled, `hinge(solid, axis, through,\nat)` declares a revolute joint and poses it, and `obstacle(solid, name)` adds what the\nparts mount into: the machine, the wall, the shelf above. The joint angle is an\nordinary keyword default, so the viewer's slider swings it live, and the slider ends\nexactly where the declared range does.\n\n**The declared range is a claim, and `nurb check` audits it** the way min_wall audits\na wall: each hinge sweeps through it against everything else in the scene, and a\nfinding is the angle where it jams plus the coordinates of the contact. Declare what\nthe design needs, never what happens to pass. A door that must stay open by gravity\nneeds past 90 degrees; declaring (0, 90) because that sweeps clean is writing the test\nto match the bug.\n\n**Nothing full width may cross the pivot line.** The mount that carries a hinge has to\nreach the pin from somewhere, so some of it always lives above or behind the pin, and\nany full-width material on the moving part that reaches past the pivot sweeps straight\ninto it. The door that jammed at 45 did so against its own top edge, carried past the\npin to support the knuckles; the knuckles got narrow tabs instead, sized to pass\nbeside the mount, and the panel now starts at the pivot line.\n\n**Obstacles are boxes and prisms, never thin hand-drawn profiles.** Three nearly\ncollinear points make a razor sliver, and OCCT answers a boolean against a degenerate\nsolid with chunks of the other operand: measured once as a 152,000mm3 phantom\ncollision at a pose that was actually clear. The sweep refuses any intersection that\nis not a subset of its inputs and names the solid to fix, but the fix is to model the\nobstacle as something with honest volume in the first place.\n\n**Tangent is clear, and clear is not clearance.** Collision is intersection volume, so\ntwo faces that kiss at zero volume pass, the closed door resting on its stop included.\nIn plastic a zero-clearance pass is already a bind. The declared range should carry\nthe same honesty about clearance that a tongue's `fit` carries about width. The fits\ntable puts numbers to that honesty: 0.3mm is the least a moving pair carries through\nits whole travel, and 0.5mm is what never binds.\n\n**The stop the sweep finds can be the detent the design wants.** The door that\nmotivated all of this rests open at 240 degrees against the back of its own mount,\nheld there by gravity, and that contact is a feature with a card entry, not a finding\nto engineer away. Read a jam before redesigning around it.\n\n**Never trust a swing worked out by hand.** The same hinge was hand-modelled three times and gave three answers, one of them \"impossible\"; the wrong one ran a convex test against a non-convex profile, which is exactly the kind of quiet modelling error a kernel boolean cannot make. The sweep is the authority.\n\n**The sweep is priced per pose, and the declaration sets the pose count.** Every step is a kernel boolean against the rest of the scene, so a door walking 90 degrees at the default 3-degree step is cheap, while a full-circle rotor at the same step is 120 poses and can hold the check for seconds on real geometry. A clean sweep pays the whole walk, since only a jam stops it early. `through=(0, 360)` at the default step is a fine-grained jam audit, not a formality: a free spinner that only needs a gross clearance check should declare a larger `step`, and a range wider than the design actually claims buys nothing but poses.\n\nOne hinge sweeps at a time; the others hold their pose, which is the conservative\nreading of a mechanism you can only move one hand at a time. Printability rules stay\noff assemblies entirely: each part already answered them alone, and overhang measured\non an assembled scene reports confident nonsense.\n\n## Verification\n\n\"It built\" is not verification. `nurb verify` runs the machine-checkable part of\nthis list: one solid per configuration, every count flexed upward, the rules clean,\nand the card agreeing with the geometry. `--report` writes the verdict into\n`build/renders/<part>.verify.md` with the renders that back it beside it, one still\nper finding. The two it cannot do are the two that need you, and they are items 2 and 6.\n\nBefore presenting a part:\n\n1. **Flex the driving parameters up as well as down**, for example 4 to 6 to 2 to 4.\n   Growth is what catches a frozen selector; shrinking alone passes a broken part.\n2. **Check fit-critical faces by coordinate** after any polish or resize. `nurb inspect`\n   lists them, with each finding resolved to the face it fired on. Which faces are\n   fit-critical is still yours to know, which is why this is not something `nurb verify`\n   can run for you.\n3. **Confirm the solid count**, which is almost always one.\n4. **Run `nurb check`.** Zero findings is the bar, and a finding fired at a part that\n   prints fine is a bug in the rule, not something to accept quietly.\n5. **Predict a baseline before you look at it.** Working out what the sliver count\n   should be from the polish exclusions turns the number into a test of the rule instead\n   of something to write down.\n6. **Render it and actually look.** `nurb render <part>` writes a PNG, `--section\n   z:4mm` cuts it open where outside views cannot reach, and `nurb inspect --render`\n   stands a camera at every finding with the guilty face painted. A part can pass\n   every numeric check and still be visibly wrong.\n\n"}}],"rawOutput":{"type":"Bash","output":[],"output_for_prompt":" same shelf sized for the wide bin: three columns instead of two.\"\n\n[variants.shelf_gridfinity_3x2.params]\ngrid_x = 3\nbracket_count = 6\n\n[variants.shelf_gridfinity_3x2.accepted]\nsliver = 26\n```\n\nThe test is whether it is the same geometry. Record what you are told in\n`measurements.toml` at the project root, with how it was obtained, and read it with\n`measured()`:\n\n```toml\n[shelf_depth]\nvalue = 340\nunit = \"mm\"\nhow = \"tape measure, freezer middle shelf, 2026-07-20\"\n```\n\n```python\nfrom nurb import measured\n\ndepth = measured(\"shelf_depth\")\n```\n\nAn unknown name raises, naming what is on file. That failure is the point: it is the\nmoment to ask rather than to pick something plausible.\n\n**A published number is a measurement, not a guess.** When the part mates with a manufactured product or a published standard, a VESA mount, a gridfinity bin, a camera thread, the number already exists in a datasheet, and making somebody caliper a hole pattern a standards body fixed is friction wearing rigor's clothes. Research it, record it like any other measurement with `how` naming the source (\"VESA MIS-D 100, manufacturer product page\"), and ask only for what nobody published, like the opening the finished thing has to fit. Two limits keep this honest: the user's actual object outranks the spec when the two disagree, because clones drift, and a number inferred from a product photo or a listing's marketing copy was never published at all, so it is a guess and gets marked like one.\n\n**A photo is a shape, never a dimension.** It can identify the standard, that the siding is dutch lap, that the rail is 2020 extrusion, and the published profile carries the numbers from there. Pixels carry no millimetres, so a dimension read off a photo is a guess and gets marked like one.\n\n**A phone scan is reference geometry, not metrology.** Its error changes with the phone, capture mode, surface and technique, so no universal millimetre threshold makes it a caliper. `nurb scan` reads the mesh in mm, states the units it used, and slices profile polylines to sketch against. Record what it gave with `how` naming the file and the slice, and keep every scan-derived fit `provisional` until a coupon proves it against the real object.\n\n**A fit coupon turns a loose measurement into a tight one.** Before printing a part modelled against a scan or a photo, print the mating surface alone: a thin strip carrying just the profile, minutes of filament. Held against the real object it shows every gap the numbers hid, the parameters get corrected, and only then does the full part print. A coupon that fits is what takes the provisional flag off.\n\n**When there is nobody to ask**, write the guess down and mark it `provisional = true`.\nThe danger was never the guess, it is that a guess and a measurement look identical six\nmonths later. `how` is still required, because \"eyeballed against a broom\" tells the\nnext person how far to trust it, and `nurb check` lists every provisional value until\nsomebody picks up a caliper.\n\nA measured value pays for itself across a family. Notch measured one bracket pitch and\namortized it over sixteen parts.\n\n## Assemblies\n\nEvery rule above judges one solid being manufactured. An assembly judges solids being\nused together: a door on its mount, a lid over the machine it covers. The failure it\nexists for built clean, checked clean, exported watertight and printed beautifully,\nthen jammed at 45 degrees of its swing, because the collision between two correct\nparts existed only in the physical world. No per-solid rule can have an opinion about\nmotion.\n\nThe contract mirrors a part's. An assembly is a function in `parts/` whose keyword\ndefaults are its parameters; what it returns is placed solids rather than one solid.\n`use(name)` builds a sibling part where it was modelled, `hinge(solid, axis, through,\nat)` declares a revolute joint and poses it, and `obstacle(solid, name)` adds what the\nparts mount into: the machine, the wall, the shelf above. The joint angle is an\nordinary keyword default, so the viewer's slider swings it live, and the slider ends\nexactly where the declared range does.\n\n**The declared range is a claim, and `nurb check` audits it** the way min_wall audits\na wall: each hinge sweeps through it against everything else in the scene, and a\nfinding is the angle where it jams plus the coordinates of the contact. Declare what\nthe design needs, never what happens to pass. A door that must stay open by gravity\nneeds past 90 degrees; declaring (0, 90) because that sweeps clean is writing the test\nto match the bug.\n\n**Nothing full width may cross the pivot line.** The mount that carries a hinge has to\nreach the pin from somewhere, so some of it always lives above or behind the pin, and\nany full-width material on the moving part that reaches past the pivot sweeps straight\ninto it. The door that jammed at 45 did so against its own top edge, carried past the\npin to support the knuckles; the knuckles got narrow tabs instead, sized to pass\nbeside the mount, and the panel now starts at the pivot line.\n\n**Obstacles are boxes and prisms, never thin hand-drawn profiles.** Three nearly\ncollinear points make a razor sliver, and OCCT answers a boolean against a degenerate\nsolid with chunks of the other operand: measured once as a 152,000mm3 phantom\ncollision at a pose that was actually clear. The sweep refuses any intersection that\nis not a subset of its inputs and names the solid to fix, but the fix is to model the\nobstacle as something with honest volume in the first place.\n\n**Tangent is clear, and clear is not clearance.** Collision is intersection volume, so\ntwo faces that kiss at zero volume pass, the closed door resting on its stop included.\nIn plastic a zero-clearance pass is already a bind. The declared range should carry\nthe same honesty about clearance that a tongue's `fit` carries about width. The fits\ntable puts numbers to that honesty: 0.3mm is the least a moving pair carries through\nits whole travel, and 0.5mm is what never binds.\n\n**The stop the sweep finds can be the detent the design wants.** The door that\nmotivated all of this rests open at 240 degrees against the back of its own mount,\nheld there by gravity, and that contact is a feature with a card entry, not a finding\nto engineer away. Read a jam before redesigning around it.\n\n**Never trust a swing worked out by hand.** The same hinge was hand-modelled three times and gave three answers, one of them \"impossible\"; the wrong one ran a convex test against a non-convex profile, which is exactly the kind of quiet modelling error a kernel boolean cannot make. The sweep is the authority.\n\n**The sweep is priced per pose, and the declaration sets the pose count.** Every step is a kernel boolean against the rest of the scene, so a door walking 90 degrees at the default 3-degree step is cheap, while a full-circle rotor at the same step is 120 poses and can hold the check for seconds on real geometry. A clean sweep pays the whole walk, since only a jam stops it early. `through=(0, 360)` at the default step is a fine-grained jam audit, not a formality: a free spinner that only needs a gross clearance check should declare a larger `step`, and a range wider than the design actually claims buys nothing but poses.\n\nOne hinge sweeps at a time; the others hold their pose, which is the conservative\nreading of a mechanism you can only move one hand at a time. Printability rules stay\noff assemblies entirely: each part already answered them alone, and overhang measured\non an assembled scene reports confident nonsense.\n\n## Verification\n\n\"It built\" is not verification. `nurb verify` runs the machine-checkable part of\nthis list: one solid per configuration, every count flexed upward, the rules clean,\nand the card agreeing with the geometry. `--report` writes the verdict into\n`build/renders/<part>.verify.md` with the renders that back it beside it, one still\nper finding. The two it cannot do are the two that need you, and they are items 2 and 6.\n\nBefore presenting a part:\n\n1. **Flex the driving parameters up as well as down**, for example 4 to 6 to 2 to 4.\n   Growth is what catches a frozen selector; shrinking alone passes a broken part.\n2. **Check fit-critical faces by coordinate** after any polish or resize. `nurb inspect`\n   lists them, with each finding resolved to the face it fired on. Which faces are\n   fit-critical is still yours to know, which is why this is not something `nurb verify`\n   can run for you.\n3. **Confirm the solid count**, which is almost always one.\n4. **Run `nurb check`.** Zero findings is the bar, and a finding fired at a part that\n   prints fine is a bug in the rule, not something to accept quietly.\n5. **Predict a baseline before you look at it.** Working out what the sliver count\n   should be from the polish exclusions turns the number into a test of the rule instead\n   of something to write down.\n6. **Render it and actually look.** `nurb render <part>` writes a PNG, `--section\n   z:4mm` cuts it open where outside views cannot reach, and `nurb inspect --render`\n   stands a camera at every finding with the guilty face painted. A part can pass\n   every numeric check and still be visibly wrong.\n\n","exit_code":0,"command":"nurb rules && echo \"===== API =====\" && nurb api","truncated":true,"signal":null,"timed_out":false,"description":null,"current_dir":"/private/var/folders/lc/0cfr61jd4s581fv23shx6jbc0000gn/T/nurb-eval-trial-f7z9kktg/project","output_file":"","total_bytes":43985},"locations":[]}

{"type":"tool_call_update","toolCallId":"call-338ecf9f-b0a5-406b-989a-1dad873696e8-6","status":"completed","content":[],"rawOutput":{"type":"TaskOutput","Result":{"task_id":"call-4194e39d-da65-4a1f-a3c0-277a49735197-2","command":"nurb rules && echo \"===== API =====\" && nurb api","status":"completed","exit_code":0,"started":"2026-08-25T18:18:43Z","ended":"2026-08-25T18:19:35Z","duration_secs":52.912894,"output":"# nurb design doctrine\n\nPrinted via `nurb rules`. This file is the single source; harness files point at it\nrather than repeating it.\n\nThese are standing rules for FDM-printed parts, and several are vetoes rather than\npreferences. Most of them are physics, so they outlive any particular CAD kernel. The\nones that are specific to OCCT are marked as such and were measured, not reasoned.\n\n## The part contract\n\n```python\nfrom nurb import *\n\n@part\ndef dispenser(width=80.0, height=120.0, wall=2.0, draft=False):\n    body = Box(width, height, wall)\n    if draft:\n        return body\n    bed = body.bounding_box().min.Z\n    keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z > bed)\n    return polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n```\n\nKeyword defaults are the parameters. That one declaration feeds the agent, the CLI, the\nviewer, the tests, and any future configurator. Never add a parallel `PARAMS` dict; the\ntwo would drift.\n\n**Write a continuous dimension as a float.** The type of a default is the only thing\nthat says whether a value is a count or a measurement, and the viewer reads it: an `int`\ndefault gets a slider that steps by one, a `float` default one that moves continuously.\n`bracket_count=4` is a count and `chamfer_size=1.0` is a millimetre, so the trailing\n`.0` is doing work. Nothing else has to be declared, and there is no annotation to keep\nin sync, because the type is already there in the signature.\n\n`draft` is optional and injected by the runtime, never passed by a caller. When it is\ntrue, skip the polish pass. It is worth about 20% on a real part, not the 18x a cube\nsuggests.\n\nReturn one solid. A function that returns two loose bodies still reports a plausible\nbounding box and still exports, so nothing downstream catches it.\n\n**When a configuration cannot work, refuse it with `reject`, never a bare raise.** A holder whose hole is narrower than the tool it holds should not build, and `reject(\"drill_hole_width 14 is under the 14.27mm pin vise plus print shrink: raise it above 14.77\", param=\"drill_hole_width\")` is how a part says so. The message states what is wrong and what value fixes it; `param` names the offending parameter so the viewer marks its slider. The viewer presents a refusal as a limit of the design, in amber with the last good geometry still on screen, where a bare `ValueError` arrives as a red traceback that reads as the part being broken. Guard only what would print wrong or not work at all; taste stays a slider.\n\n## Printability\n\n- **Minimum wall 2 to 3mm**, except where fit geometry says otherwise. Fit-critical\n  dimensions are already tuned; do not round them for tidiness.\n- **Print support-free. No floating features.** Parts print bottom down, building up in\n  +z, so every functional feature is grounded. A vertical extrusion or a vertical\n  through hole is self-supporting. A shelf, loop, or band floated partway up with a gap\n  underneath is not.\n- **A counterbore prints mouth toward the bed, and that floats its ceiling.** The shelf the screw head bears on is laid flat over the open pocket, and the smaller hole's first rim is a circle drawn on air; the `hole_ceiling` finding is this exact case, and it appears on any hole rising out of a bridged roof, not just screw pockets. Never answer it with supports inside a pocket nobody can clean: cut the hole with `counterbore(hole_dia, head_dia, head_depth, depth)`, which steps the transition through two sacrificial bridge layers, a slot bridged chord-to-chord across the pocket and the same slot turned ninety degrees across the first, so each layer spans only what the one before it laid and the whole stack prints support-free. Reach for it whenever a design wants a screw head, a nut, or any wider recess on the bed side of a hole.\n- **Corbel rule.** Grounded does not mean a column to the bed. Support-free means no\n  layer overhanging past 45 degrees. Where material would run to the plate only to\n  satisfy printing, carry the feature on a 45 degree underside instead: a short vertical\n  tip of 4 to 6mm below the floor at the front face, then a 45 degree plane falling back\n  into the body. Every layer then overhangs by at most half a bead and bonds to the wall\n  behind it.\n- **Corbels are always exactly 45 degrees**, the same as every other facet. Never\n  steepen one or match it to a ratio. Let the landing point fall where 45 degrees puts\n  it. Mismatched facet angles are a veto: every facet on the part, cosmetic or\n  structural or corbel, has to read as one system.\n- **A large first layer peels its corners as it cools.** Every layer shrinks as it cools and pulls toward the middle of the part, and the pull lands hardest on a sharp plan corner, farthest from the middle and holding on at a point. Past about 20,000mm2 of first layer the accumulated pull beats corner adhesion, and `warp_risk` names the corners that will lift. The fixes are in the outline, which is what makes this a CAD problem where elephant's foot is not: round the vertical corners at 8mm or more, so the peel front is a curve instead of a point, and give a big plate a ribbed floor rather than a solid slab, which is stiffer per gram and halves what contracts. A 1mm polish chamfer is not relief here; it moves the point half a millimetre. The brim and the clean bed are the slicer's share, and they treat the symptom the outline caused. Material multiplies the pull: the threshold is calibrated on PLA, and naming what the machine prints in `printer.toml`, `material = \"abs\"` next to the profile line, tightens it fivefold, because ABS contracts 1 to 2% as it cools where PLA holds under half a percent. PETG judges as PLA, ASA as ABS, and PC and PP tighter still. At the far end the rule stops being about corners: a bed-covering part in ABS, ASA or PC is the wrong material, and the fix is PETG or PLA, not a wider brim.\n- **Elephant's foot is a slicer setting**, not a CAD problem. Do not model around it.\n- **A pin under 5mm across is perimeters with nothing inside.** There is no room between the walls for infill, so a thin printed pin is a tube, loaded in bending at the weakest weld it has, its base. Under 3mm the nozzle is re-melting each ring as it lays the next, and the pin may not survive its own printing. `pin` fires on a free-standing vertical cylinder taller than twice its diameter; a stub or a locating nub has nothing to lever with and stays silent. The fixes, in order: thicken it past 5mm, give its base a structural chamfer sized like any other loaded junction, or model the hole instead and press in a metal pin, the same trade the fastener rules already make, because off-the-shelf steel beats printed plastic everywhere they compete.\n\n### Holes\n\n- **No hole under 2mm across.** Below that the perimeters converge and the bore prints as a smear or closes outright. A locating hole that small is a drill's job: model a 1mm dimple to centre the bit and let steel cut the diameter.\n- **Every vertical bore prints small**, by the same few tenths the fastener table's medium column already absorbs for screws, and the physics does not care that a dowel or a shaft is not a screw. Any bore gets the medium column's slack against its rod's true diameter, and when the diameter genuinely matters, printing is the wrong finisher: model half a millimetre under and drill to size, because a drill holds a tolerance no printer does.\n- **A horizontal hole's crown is a bridge.** Under the printer's span limit no rule minds it, but the crown sags into the bore and prints out of round exactly where a fit would bear. Prefer standing the hole vertical; the orientation rules usually allow it. When the axis cannot move and roundness matters, roof the bore with two 45 degree chords meeting in a point above the crown, a teardrop, which is the counterbore's idea turned sideways: every layer leans on the one before instead of spanning air.\n\n### Fasteners\n\n**A published standard is not a guess.** Measurements says never improvise a dimension, and a screw is the one place that rule gets misread: nobody has to measure an M3 cap screw, because ISO fixed its head at 5.5mm across in every box you will ever open. Take these from the table and spend the question you saved on something the table cannot answer.\n\n| Thread | Clearance hole, close | medium | Cap head dia | Cap head height | Nut across flats | across corners | Nut thickness |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| M2 | 2.2 | 2.4 | 3.8 | 2.0 | 4.0 | 4.4 | 1.6 |\n| M2.5 | 2.7 | 2.9 | 4.5 | 2.5 | 5.0 | 5.5 | 2.0 |\n| M3 | 3.2 | 3.4 | 5.5 | 3.0 | 5.5 | 6.1 | 2.4 |\n| M4 | 4.3 | 4.5 | 7.0 | 4.0 | 7.0 | 7.7 | 3.2 |\n| M5 | 5.3 | 5.5 | 8.5 | 5.0 | 8.0 | 8.8 | 4.7 |\n| M6 | 6.4 | 6.6 | 10.0 | 6.0 | 10.0 | 11.1 | 5.2 |\n| M8 | 8.4 | 9.0 | 13.0 | 8.0 | 13.0 | 14.4 | 6.8 |\n\nClearance is ISO 273, cap head is ISO 4762 socket head, nut is ISO 4032 hex. In mm. Across corners is the one a round pocket has to clear, and it is the number people reach for the wrong column of: an M3 nut is 5.5 across the flats and will not go into a 5.5 hole.\n\n**Reach for the medium column.** A printed hole comes out under its modelled size, by a few tenths that vary with the machine, the material and how fast the perimeter was laid, so the close column is a fit you have to earn with a coupon rather than one you can assume. Medium already carries that much slack, which is why it is the default here and close is the exception a fit coupon has justified.\n\n**Give a screw head its pocket through `counterbore`, never a plain wider hole.** Head diameter plus about 0.4, head height plus a layer, and the pocket faces the bed with the shaft rising out of it: that is the shape the table above is sized for, and it is the shape `counterbore` cuts.\n\n**A nut pocket is a hex prism, and `counterbore` cannot cut one.** It cuts a cylinder, so the pocket is modelled by hand: `extrude(RegularPolygon(across_corners / 2, 6), thickness + 0.2)` sized on the across-corners column, or a round pocket at across-corners plus 0.2 if the nut\n\n... (output truncated) ...\n\nsame shelf sized for the wide bin: three columns instead of two.\"\n\n[variants.shelf_gridfinity_3x2.params]\ngrid_x = 3\nbracket_count = 6\n\n[variants.shelf_gridfinity_3x2.accepted]\nsliver = 26\n```\n\nThe test is whether it is the same geometry. A wider cradle on the same J is a variant.\nA different mechanism is a part, however similar the slab looks.\n\n`note` is one sentence saying why the variant exists, written in the user's words rather than the doctrine's, because the viewer shows it next to the variant and its reader is whoever is about to print the thing. The params are the how and never the why: `diagonal = true` explains nothing to someone who has not read the doctrine, and \"prints tilted so it needs no supports\" does.\n\n## Measurements\n\nThe bottleneck on a one-off is not geometry, it is dimensions. A wrong number produces a\nperfect model of the wrong object, and nothing downstream can catch it.\n\n**Ask for a measurement. Never improvise one.** A guessed clearance that happens to\nbuild is worse than a failure, because it prints. Record what you are told in\n`measurements.toml` at the project root, with how it was obtained, and read it with\n`measured()`:\n\n```toml\n[shelf_depth]\nvalue = 340\nunit = \"mm\"\nhow = \"tape measure, freezer middle shelf, 2026-07-20\"\n```\n\n```python\nfrom nurb import measured\n\ndepth = measured(\"shelf_depth\")\n```\n\nAn unknown name raises, naming what is on file. That failure is the point: it is the\nmoment to ask rather than to pick something plausible.\n\n**A published number is a measurement, not a guess.** When the part mates with a manufactured product or a published standard, a VESA mount, a gridfinity bin, a camera thread, the number already exists in a datasheet, and making somebody caliper a hole pattern a standards body fixed is friction wearing rigor's clothes. Research it, record it like any other measurement with `how` naming the source (\"VESA MIS-D 100, manufacturer product page\"), and ask only for what nobody published, like the opening the finished thing has to fit. Two limits keep this honest: the user's actual object outranks the spec when the two disagree, because clones drift, and a number inferred from a product photo or a listing's marketing copy was never published at all, so it is a guess and gets marked like one.\n\n**A photo is a shape, never a dimension.** It can identify the standard, that the siding is dutch lap, that the rail is 2020 extrusion, and the published profile carries the numbers from there. Pixels carry no millimetres, so a dimension read off a photo is a guess and gets marked like one.\n\n**A phone scan is reference geometry, not metrology.** Its error changes with the phone, capture mode, surface and technique, so no universal millimetre threshold makes it a caliper. `nurb scan` reads the mesh in mm, states the units it used, and slices profile polylines to sketch against. Record what it gave with `how` naming the file and the slice, and keep every scan-derived fit `provisional` until a coupon proves it against the real object.\n\n**A fit coupon turns a loose measurement into a tight one.** Before printing a part modelled against a scan or a photo, print the mating surface alone: a thin strip carrying just the profile, minutes of filament. Held against the real object it shows every gap the numbers hid, the parameters get corrected, and only then does the full part print. A coupon that fits is what takes the provisional flag off.\n\n**When there is nobody to ask**, write the guess down and mark it `provisional = true`.\nThe danger was never the guess, it is that a guess and a measurement look identical six\nmonths later. `how` is still required, because \"eyeballed against a broom\" tells the\nnext person how far to trust it, and `nurb check` lists every provisional value until\nsomebody picks up a caliper.\n\nA measured value pays for itself across a family. Notch measured one bracket pitch and\namortized it over sixteen parts.\n\n## Assemblies\n\nEvery rule above judges one solid being manufactured. An assembly judges solids being\nused together: a door on its mount, a lid over the machine it covers. The failure it\nexists for built clean, checked clean, exported watertight and printed beautifully,\nthen jammed at 45 degrees of its swing, because the collision between two correct\nparts existed only in the physical world. No per-solid rule can have an opinion about\nmotion.\n\nThe contract mirrors a part's. An assembly is a function in `parts/` whose keyword\ndefaults are its parameters; what it returns is placed solids rather than one solid.\n`use(name)` builds a sibling part where it was modelled, `hinge(solid, axis, through,\nat)` declares a revolute joint and poses it, and `obstacle(solid, name)` adds what the\nparts mount into: the machine, the wall, the shelf above. The joint angle is an\nordinary keyword default, so the viewer's slider swings it live, and the slider ends\nexactly where the declared range does.\n\n**The declared range is a claim, and `nurb check` audits it** the way min_wall audits\na wall: each hinge sweeps through it against everything else in the scene, and a\nfinding is the angle where it jams plus the coordinates of the contact. Declare what\nthe design needs, never what happens to pass. A door that must stay open by gravity\nneeds past 90 degrees; declaring (0, 90) because that sweeps clean is writing the test\nto match the bug.\n\n**Nothing full width may cross the pivot line.** The mount that carries a hinge has to\nreach the pin from somewhere, so some of it always lives above or behind the pin, and\nany full-width material on the moving part that reaches past the pivot sweeps straight\ninto it. The door that jammed at 45 did so against its own top edge, carried past the\npin to support the knuckles; the knuckles got narrow tabs instead, sized to pass\nbeside the mount, and the panel now starts at the pivot line.\n\n**Obstacles are boxes and prisms, never thin hand-drawn profiles.** Three nearly\ncollinear points make a razor sliver, and OCCT answers a boolean against a degenerate\nsolid with chunks of the other operand: measured once as a 152,000mm3 phantom\ncollision at a pose that was actually clear. The sweep refuses any intersection that\nis not a subset of its inputs and names the solid to fix, but the fix is to model the\nobstacle as something with honest volume in the first place.\n\n**Tangent is clear, and clear is not clearance.** Collision is intersection volume, so\ntwo faces that kiss at zero volume pass, the closed door resting on its stop included.\nIn plastic a zero-clearance pass is already a bind. The declared range should carry\nthe same honesty about clearance that a tongue's `fit` carries about width. The fits\ntable puts numbers to that honesty: 0.3mm is the least a moving pair carries through\nits whole travel, and 0.5mm is what never binds.\n\n**The stop the sweep finds can be the detent the design wants.** The door that\nmotivated all of this rests open at 240 degrees against the back of its own mount,\nheld there by gravity, and that contact is a feature with a card entry, not a finding\nto engineer away. Read a jam before redesigning around it.\n\n**Never trust a swing worked out by hand.** The same hinge was hand-modelled three times and gave three answers, one of them \"impossible\"; the wrong one ran a convex test against a non-convex profile, which is exactly the kind of quiet modelling error a kernel boolean cannot make. The sweep is the authority.\n\n**The sweep is priced per pose, and the declaration sets the pose count.** Every step is a kernel boolean against the rest of the scene, so a door walking 90 degrees at the default 3-degree step is cheap, while a full-circle rotor at the same step is 120 poses and can hold the check for seconds on real geometry. A clean sweep pays the whole walk, since only a jam stops it early. `through=(0, 360)` at the default step is a fine-grained jam audit, not a formality: a free spinner that only needs a gross clearance check should declare a larger `step`, and a range wider than the design actually claims buys nothing but poses.\n\nOne hinge sweeps at a time; the others hold their pose, which is the conservative\nreading of a mechanism you can only move one hand at a time. Printability rules stay\noff assemblies entirely: each part already answered them alone, and overhang measured\non an assembled scene reports confident nonsense.\n\n## Verification\n\n\"It built\" is not verification. `nurb verify` runs the machine-checkable part of\nthis list: one solid per configuration, every count flexed upward, the rules clean,\nand the card agreeing with the geometry. `--report` writes the verdict into\n`build/renders/<part>.verify.md` with the renders that back it beside it, one still\nper finding. The two it cannot do are the two that need you, and they are items 2 and 6.\n\nBefore presenting a part:\n\n1. **Flex the driving parameters up as well as down**, for example 4 to 6 to 2 to 4.\n   Growth is what catches a frozen selector; shrinking alone passes a broken part.\n2. **Check fit-critical faces by coordinate** after any polish or resize. `nurb inspect`\n   lists them, with each finding resolved to the face it fired on. Which faces are\n   fit-critical is still yours to know, which is why this is not something `nurb verify`\n   can run for you.\n3. **Confirm the solid count**, which is almost always one.\n4. **Run `nurb check`.** Zero findings is the bar, and a finding fired at a part that\n   prints fine is a bug in the rule, not something to accept quietly.\n5. **Predict a baseline before you look at it.** Working out what the sliver count\n   should be from the polish exclusions turns the number into a test of the rule instead\n   of something to write down.\n6. **Render it and actually look.** `nurb render <part>` writes a PNG, `--section\n   z:4mm` cuts it open where outside views cannot reach, and `nurb inspect --render`\n   stands a camera at every finding with the guilty face painted. A part can pass\n   every numeric check and still be visibly wrong.\n\n===== API =====\n  from nurb import *  gives a part file all of build123d, plus:\n\n  part(fn)\n      Mark a function as a part.\n  reject(message, param=None)\n      Refuse to build a configuration the part knows cannot work.\n  is_convex(edge, f1, f2)\n      True if the material folds away from itself across this edge.\n  concave_edges(shape)\n      Every concave edge, which is where polish is forbidden and stress collects.\n  measured(name, start=None)\n      A measured value, in mm.\n  polish(shape, edges, size)\n      Chamfer as much of `edges` as will land, and stop there.\n  crown(wall, radius=None)\n      Round the top of a closed perimeter wall with one smooth bead, on request.\n  stand(shape, tilt=45.0, axis=Axis((0, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)), facet=2.0, fins=True)\n      Tilt a part for diagonal printing and shave a flat for it to stand on.\n  counterbore(hole_dia, head_dia, head_depth, depth, layer=1.0)\n      The negative space of a counterbored hole whose ceiling prints without support.\n  assembly(fn)\n      Mark a function as an assembly. Its keyword defaults are parameters, exactly\n  use(name, **overrides)\n      Build a sibling part by name and return its solid, placed where it was modelled.\n  hinge(solid, axis, through, at=0.0, name=None, step=3.0)\n      Declare that this solid rotates about `axis`, and pose it at `at` degrees.\n  obstacle(solid, name='an obstacle')\n      Context geometry: the wall, the machine, the shelf above.\n\n  And it replaces these build123d names with its own. This file is the single source; harness files point at it\nrather than repeating it.\n\nThese are standing rules for FDM-printed parts, and several are vetoes rather than\npreferences. Most of them are physics, so they outlive any particular CAD kernel. The\nones that are specific to OCCT are marked as such and were measured, not reasoned.\n\n10→## The part contract\n\n```python\nfrom nurb import *\n\n@part\ndef dispenser(width=80.0, height=120.0, wall=2.0, draft=False):\n    body = Box(width, height, wall)\n    if draft:\n        return body\n20→    bed = body.bounding_box().min.Z\n    keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z > bed)\n    return polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n```\n\nKeyword defaults are the parameters. That one declaration feeds the agent, the CLI, the\nviewer, the tests, and any future configurator. Never add a parallel `PARAMS` dict; the\ntwo would drift.\n\n**Write a continuous dimension as a float.** The type of a default is the only thing\n30→that says whether a value is a count or a measurement, and the viewer reads it: an `int`\ndefault gets a slider that steps by one, a `float` default one that moves continuously.\n`bracket_count=4` is a count and `chamfer_size=1.0` is a millimetre, so the trailing\n`.0` is doing work. Nothing else has to be declared, and there is no annotation to keep\nin sync, because the type is already there in the signature.\n\n`draft` is optional and injected by the runtime, never passed by a caller. When it is\ntrue, skip the polish pass. It is worth about 20% on a real part, not the 18x a cube\nsuggests.\n\n40→Return one solid. A function that returns two loose bodies still reports a plausible\nbounding box and still exports, so nothing downstream catches it.\n\n**When a configuration cannot work, refuse it with `reject`, never a bare raise.** A holder whose hole is narrower than the tool it holds should not build, and `reject(\"drill_hole_width 14 is under the 14.27mm pin vise plus print shrink: raise it above 14.77\", param=\"drill_hole_width\")` is how a part says so. The message states what is wrong and what value fixes it; `param` names the offending parameter so the viewer marks its slider. The viewer presents a refusal as a limit of the design, in amber with the last good geometry still on screen, where a bare `ValueError` arrives as a red traceback that reads as the part being broken. Guard only what would print wrong or not work at all; taste stays a slider.\n\n## Printability\n\n- **Minimum wall 2 to 3mm**, except where fit geometry says otherwise. Fit-critical\n  dimensions are already tuned; do not round them for tidiness.\n- **Print support-free. No floating features.** Parts print bottom down, building up in\n50→  +z, so every functional feature is grounded. return \"\"\n\n\ndef _signature(obj):\n40→    try:\n        return f\"{obj.__name__}{inspect.signature(obj)}\"\n    except (TypeError, ValueError):  # a C function, or anything without one\n        return getattr(obj, \"__name__\", str(obj))\n\n\ndef _b3d_names(build123d):\n    return set(getattr(build123d, \"__all__\", ()) or dir(build123d))\n\n\n50→def own_names():\n    \"\"\"What `nurb` adds to build123d, in the order `__init__` declares it.\"\"\"\n    import build123d\n\n    import nurb\n\n    return [n for n in nurb.__all__ if n not in _b3d_names(build123d)]\n\n\ndef return lines\n\n\ndef report():\n    own, shadowed, borrowed = entries()\n    lines = [\"  from nurb import *  gives a part file all of build123d, plus:\", \"\"]\n    for sig, summary in own:\n {"type":"tool_call_update","toolCallId":"call-4520dda2-f69a-49b6-9265-0841b75c1024-17","status":"completed","content":[{"type":"content","content":{"type":"text","text":"1→\"\"\"Named real-world values, with provenance.\n\nThe bottleneck on a one-off part is not geometry, it is dimensions. An agent cannot\nmeasure a freezer shelf, and a guessed number produces a perfect model of the wrong\nobject: it builds, it checks clean, and it prints. Nothing downstream catches it.\n\nSo a measurement is a named value on disk with a note saying how it was obtained, and\nasking for one that is not on file raises. That failure is the feature. It is the moment\nto ask rather than to pick something plausible.\n10→\"\"\"\n\nimport pathlib\nimport sys\nimport tomllib\n\nFILENAME = \"measurements.toml\"\n\n\nclass MeasurementError(LookupError):\n20→    \"\"\"A measurement is missing or unusable.\n\n    Not `KeyError`, which reprs its argument: a message with a worked example in it comes\n    out as one quoted string full of backslash-n, and the example is the useful part.\n    \"\"\"\n\n\ndef _caller_dir(depth):\n    \"\"\"Where the code that called us lives, so the lookup needs no configuration.\"\"\"\n    frame = sys._getframe(depth)\n30→    here = frame.f_globals.get(\"__file__\")\n    return pathlib.Path(here).resolve().parent if here else pathlib.Path.cwd()\n\n\ndef _find(start):\n    \"\"\"The nearest measurements file, without leaving the project.\n\n    The walk stops at the project root, meaning the directory holding `parts/`. Without\n    that stop it would keep going to the filesystem root and could silently answer with\n    some unrelated file from an ancestor directory, which is the exact failure this whole\n40→    module exists to prevent: a dimension that is wrong and looks fine.\n    \"\"\"\n    for d in [start, *start.parents]:\n        if (d / FILENAME).is_file():\n            return d / FILENAME\n        if (d / \"parts\").is_dir():\n            return None\n    return None\n\n\n50→def _read(path):\n    \"\"\"Parse it, and say which file when it will not parse. The same courtesy cards get.\"\"\"\n    try:\n        return tomllib.loads(path.read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\"))\n    except tomllib.TOMLDecodeError as exc:\n        raise MeasurementError(f\"{path.name}: not valid TOML ({exc})\") from exc\n\n\ndef load(start=None):\n    \"\"\"Every measurement on file, as name -> record. Empty when there is no file.\"\"\"\n60→    path = _find(pathlib.Path(start).resolve() if start else _caller_dir(2))\n    return _read(path) if path else {}\n\n\ndef provisional(start=None):\n    \"\"\"Every value on file that admits it was not actually measured.\n\n    The doctrine says to ask rather than improvise, and sometimes there is nobody to\n    ask: the caliper is in a drawer, the object is at the office, the print has to go\n    on tonight. The failure mode is not putting a number in, it is that the number then\n70→    looks exactly like one somebody measured. Six months later nothing distinguishes\n    them and the part is wrong for a reason no one can find.\n\n    So a guess is allowed to be written down and required to say so, and `nurb check`\n    reports the ones that still are. `how` stays mandatory either way: a provisional\n    value still has to say where it came from, because \"eyeballed against a broom\"\n    tells the next person how much to trust it.\n    \"\"\"\n    return sorted(\n        (name, entry.get(\"how\", \"\"))\n80→        for name, entry in load(start).items()\n        if entry.get(\"provisional\")\n    )\n\n\ndef measured(name, start=None):\n    \"\"\"A measured value, in mm.\n\n    Raises when it is not on file, when it has no provenance, or when it is recorded in\n    units this does not work in. All three are cases where continuing would produce\n90→    geometry that looks right and is wrong.\n\n    A value marked `provisional = true` is returned like any other. It is a real number\n    that builds a real part; what it is not is measured, and `nurb check` says so until\n    somebody picks up a caliper.\n    \"\"\"\n    start = pathlib.Path(start).resolve() if start else _caller_dir(2)\n    path = _find(start)\n    if path is None:\n        raise MeasurementError(\n100→            f\"no {FILENAME} above {start}, so there is nothing measured to ask for. \"\n            f\"Measure {name!r}, then record it:\\n\\n\"\n            f'  [{name}]\\n  value = 0\\n  unit = \"mm\"\\n  how = \"how you measured it\"\\n\\n'\n            f\"If there is nobody to ask right now, add `provisional = true` and put \"\n            f\"your best guess in. `nurb check` will keep reminding you.\"\n        )\n    book = _read(path)\n    if name not in book:\n        have = \", \".join(sorted(book)) or \"nothing yet\"\n        raise MeasurementError(\n110→            f\"nothing measured called {name!r} in {path.name}. have: {have}. \"\n            f\"Ask for the measurement rather than guessing one: a wrong number here \"\n            f\"builds, checks clean, and prints.\"\n        )\n    entry = book[name]\n    if \"value\" not in entry:\n        raise MeasurementError(f\"{path.name}: {name} has no value\")\n    if \"how\" not in entry:\n        raise MeasurementError(\n            f\"{path.name}: {name} does not say how it was measured. A value without \"\n120→            f\"provenance is a guess with a filename on it.\"","absolute_path":"/private/var/folders/lc/0cfr61jd4s581fv23shx6jbc0000gn/T/nurb-eval-trial-f7z9kktg/runtime/venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/nurb/measurements.py","offset":null,"limit":120,"raw_output":"\"\"\"Named real-world values, with provenance.\n\nThe bottleneck on a one-off part is not geometry, it is dimensions. An agent cannot\nmeasure a freezer shelf, and a guessed number produces a perfect model of the wrong\nobject: it builds, it checks clean, and it prints. Nothing downstream catches it.\n\nSo a measurement is a named value on disk with a note saying how it was obtained, and\nasking for one that is not on file raises. That failure is the feature. It is the moment\nto ask rather than to pick something plausible.\n\"\"\"\n\nimport pathlib\nimport sys\nimport tomllib\n\nFILENAME = \"measurements.toml\"\n\n\nclass MeasurementError(LookupError):\n    \"\"\"A measurement is missing or unusable.\n\n    Not `KeyError`, which reprs its argument: a message with a worked example in it comes\n    out as one quoted string full of backslash-n, and the example is the useful part.\n    \"\"\"\n\n\ndef _caller_dir(depth):\n    \"\"\"Where the code that called us lives, so the lookup needs no configuration.\"\"\"\n    frame = sys._getframe(depth)\n    here = frame.f_globals.get(\"__file__\")\n    return pathlib.Path(here).resolve().parent if here else pathlib.Path.cwd()\n\n\ndef _find(start):\n    \"\"\"The nearest measurements file, without leaving the project.\n\n    The walk stops at the project root, meaning the directory holding `parts/`. Without\n    that stop it would keep going to the filesystem root and could silently answer with\n    some unrelated file from an ancestor directory, which is the exact failure this whole\n    module exists to prevent: a dimension that is wrong and looks fine.\n    \"\"\"\n    for d in [start, *start.parents]:\n        if (d / FILENAME).is_file():\n            return d / FILENAME\n        if (d / \"parts\").is_dir():\n            return None\n    return None\n\n\ndef _read(path):\n    \"\"\"Parse it, and say which file when it will not parse. The same courtesy cards get.\"\"\"\n    try:\n        return tomllib.loads(path.read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\"))\n    except tomllib.TOMLDecodeError as exc:\n        raise MeasurementError(f\"{path.name}: not valid TOML ({exc})\") from exc\n\n\ndef load(start=None):\n    \"\"\"Every measurement on file, as name -> record. Empty when there is no file.\"\"\"\n    path = _find(pathlib.Path(start).resolve() if start else _caller_dir(2))\n    return _read(path) if path else {}\n\n\ndef provisional(start=None):\n    \"\"\"Every value on file that admits it was not actually measured.\n\n    The doctrine says to ask rather than improvise, and sometimes there is nobody to\n    ask: the caliper is in a drawer, the object is at the office, the print has to go\n    on tonight. The failure mode is not putting a number in, it is that the number then\n    looks exactly like one somebody measured. Six months later nothing distinguishes\n    them and the part is wrong for a reason no one can find.\n\n    So a guess is allowed to be written down and required to say so, and `nurb check`\n    reports the ones that still are. `how` stays mandatory either way: a provisional\n    value still has to say where it came from, because \"eyeballed against a broom\"\n    tells the next person how much to trust it.\n    \"\"\"\n    return sorted(\n        (name, entry.get(\"how\", \"\"))\n        for name, entry in load(start).items()\n        if entry.get(\"provisional\")\n    )\n\n\ndef measured(name, start=None):\n    \"\"\"A measured value, in mm.\n\n    Raises when it is not on file, when it has no provenance, or when it is recorded in\n    units this does not work in. It is a real number\n    that builds a real part; what it is not is measured, and `nurb check` says so until\n    somebody picks up a caliper.\n    \"\"\"\n    start = pathlib.Path(start).resolve() if start else _caller_dir(2)\n    path = _find(start)\n    if path is None:\n        raise MeasurementError(\n            f\"no {FILENAME} above {start}, so there is nothing measured to ask for. \"\n            f\"Measure {name!r}, then record it:\\n\\n\"\n            f'  [{name}]\\n  value = 0\\n  unit = \"mm\"\\n  how = \"how you measured it\"\\n\\n'\n            f\"If there is nobody to ask right now, add `provisional = true` and put \"\n            f\"your best guess in. `nurb check` will keep reminding you.\"\n        )\n    book = _read(path)\n    if name not in book:\n        have = \", \".join(sorted(book)) or \"nothing yet\"\n        raise MeasurementError(\n            f\"nothing measured called {name!r} in {path.name}. have: {have}. \"\n            f\"Ask for the measurement rather than guessing one: a wrong number here \"\n            f\"builds, checks clean, and prints.\"\n        )\n    entry = book[name]\n    if \"value\" not in entry:\n        raise MeasurementError(f\"{path.name}: {name} has no value\")\n    if \"how\" not in entry:\n        raise MeasurementError(\n            f\"{path.name}: {name} does not say how it was measured. {"type":"tool_call_update","toolCallId":"call-6bd1b9ca-2f8c-47a1-bb7c-251b2fe52a72-21","status":"completed","content":[{"type":"content","content":{"type":"text","text":"1→\"\"\"nurb -- agentic CAD for 3D printing.\n\nA part file needs one import:\n\n    from nurb import *\n\n    @part\n    def dispenser(width=80, height=120, wall=2):\n        return Box(width, height, wall)\n10→\"\"\"\n\nimport importlib.metadata as _metadata\n\nimport build123d as _b3d\nfrom build123d import *  # noqa: F401,F403  -- geometry vocabulary\n\nfrom .assembly import assembly, hinge, obstacle, use  # noqa: E402\nfrom .checks import concave_edges, is_convex  # noqa: E402\nfrom .crown import crown  # noqa: E402\n20→from .holes import counterbore  # noqa: E402\nfrom .measurements import measured  # noqa: E402\nfrom .mesh import import_stl  # noqa: E402  -- must win, see below\nfrom .orient import stand  # noqa: E402\nfrom .polish import chamfer, polish  # noqa: E402  -- must win, see below\nfrom .registry import part, reject  # noqa: E402  -- must win over any build123d name\n\n# `polish` is here because the doctrine prescribes the algorithm and every project\n# would otherwise write it: chamfer is all or nothing, so one edge that cannot land\n# takes the pass down and the set gets narrowed by hand until it builds.\n30→# `from nurb import *` hands a part file the whole build123d vocabulary, @part, the\n# convexity test, and `measured`. The convexity test is here because a polish pass cannot\n# be written without it: chamfering an inside corner is the one polish mistake that looks\n# fine in code. `measured` is here because the alternative to asking for a dimension is\n# inventing one, and an invented one builds, checks clean and prints.\n# `stand` is here because a diagonal print variant cannot be written without it: the\n# rotation is trivial, but the bed facet it cuts is a doctrine rule (2mm of flat, or the\n# first layer is one extrusion line wide and peels), and a part file left to tilt by\n# hand ships the knife edge.\n# `crown` is here because rounding a variable-height rim by hand is an eight-step sweep\n40→# construction (issue #55), and every direct fillet of such a rim dies in OCCT's corner\n# capping. It is the doctrine's one sanctioned round-edge treatment.\n# `counterbore` is here because the naive alternative is two cylinders that build,\n# check as an ordinary bridge, and print a screw seat on sagging air: the stepped\n# bridging stack is fixed print-farm practice, not a judgement, so it is generated.\n# `reject` is here because a part that knows a configuration cannot work (a hole\n# narrower than the tool it holds) has to be able to say so, and the alternative is a\n# bare ValueError that the viewer can only present as a crash. A refusal through\n# `reject` keeps its message and the parameter it names, and is shown as a limit of\n# the design.\n50→# `chamfer` deliberately shadows build123d's. Same behaviour, same exception type;\n# what it adds is the doctrine's rule on the way out of a failure, because the kernel's\n# own advice is \"try a smaller length value(s)\" and following it is how a part ends up\n# with a 0.4mm chamfer that lands and prints as a defect. It is the most common way a\n# part stops building, so it is the one message worth owning. `fillet` is deliberately\n# not wrapped: build123d's fillet error already names `max_fillet()` and a smaller\n# radius really is the fix there, so the chamfer rule would be wrong half the time.\n# `import_stl` shadows build123d's for a blunter reason: build123d's returns a `Face`,\n# a sheet of triangles with no inside, and subtracting from one segfaults instead of\n# raising. A part builds inside the `nurb dev` process, so the whole watcher dies\n60→# without printing anything. It is also the first name a model tries when a downloaded\n# file lands in a project. This one returns a real solid for the flat-faced meshes that\n# survive the trip, and refuses the rest pointing at `nurb scan`.\n__all__ = [\n    *getattr(_b3d, \"__all__\", [n for n in dir(_b3d) if not n.startswith(\"_\")]),\n    \"part\",\n    \"reject\",\n    \"is_convex\",\n    \"concave_edges\",\n    \"measured\",\n70→    \"polish\",\n    \"crown\",\n    \"stand\",\n    \"counterbore\",\n    \"assembly\",\n    \"use\",\n    \"hinge\",\n    \"obstacle\",\n]\n# The version lives in pyproject.toml and nowhere else; a second copy here would drift.\n80→try:"}}],"rawOutput":{"type":"ReadFile","FileContent":{"content":"1→\"\"\"nurb -- agentic CAD for 3D printing.\n\nA part file needs one import:\n\n    from nurb import *\n\n    @part\n    def dispenser(width=80, height=120, wall=2):\n        return Box(width, height, wall)\n10→\"\"\"\n\nimport importlib.metadata as _metadata\n\nimport build123d as _b3d\nfrom build123d import *  # noqa: F401,F403  -- geometry vocabulary\n\nfrom .assembly import assembly, hinge, obstacle, use  # noqa: E402\nfrom .checks import concave_edges, is_convex  # noqa: E402\nfrom .crown import crown  # noqa: E402\n20→from .holes import counterbore  # noqa: E402\nfrom .measurements import measured  # noqa: E402\nfrom .mesh import import_stl  # noqa: E402  -- must win, see below\nfrom .orient import stand  # noqa: E402\nfrom .polish import chamfer, polish  # noqa: E402  -- must win, see below\nfrom .registry import part, reject  # noqa: E402  -- must win over any build123d name\n\n# `polish` is here because the doctrine prescribes the algorithm and every project\n# would otherwise write it: chamfer is all or nothing, so one edge that cannot land\n# takes the pass down and the set gets narrowed by hand until it builds.\n30→# `from nurb import *` hands a part file the whole build123d vocabulary, @part, the\n# convexity test, and `measured`. The convexity test is here because a polish pass cannot\n# be written without it: chamfering an inside corner is the one polish mistake that looks\n# fine in code. `measured` is here because the alternative to asking for a dimension is\n# inventing one, and an invented one builds, checks clean and prints.\n# `stand` is here because a diagonal print variant cannot be written without it: the\n# rotation is trivial, but the bed facet it cuts is a doctrine rule (2mm of flat, or the\n# first layer is one extrusion line wide and peels), and a part file left to tilt by\n# hand ships the knife edge.\n# `crown` is here because rounding a variable-height rim by hand is an eight-step sweep\n40→# construction (issue #55), and every direct fillet of such a rim dies in OCCT's corner\n# capping. It is the doctrine's one sanctioned round-edge treatment.\n# `counterbore` is here because the naive alternative is two cylinders that build,\n# check as an ordinary bridge, and print a screw seat on sagging air: the stepped\n# bridging stack is fixed print-farm practice, not a judgement, so it is generated.\n# `reject` is here because a part that knows a configuration cannot work (a hole\n# narrower than the tool it holds) has to be able to say so, and the alternative is a\n# bare ValueError that the viewer can only present as a crash. A refusal through\n# `reject` keeps its message and the parameter it names, and is shown as a limit of\n# the design.\n50→# `chamfer` deliberately shadows build123d's. Same behaviour, same exception type;\n# what it adds is the doctrine's rule on the way out of a failure, because the kernel's\n# own advice is \"try a smaller length value(s)\" and following it is how a part ends up\n# with a 0.4mm chamfer that lands and prints as a defect. Clusters are gaps wider\n    # than the window itself, and the last cluster can wrap into the first.\n    clusters = [[hits[0]]]\n    for i in hits[1:]:\n        if i - clusters[-1][-1] <= window:\n            clusters[-1].append(i)\n        else:\n            clusters.append([i])\n    if len(clusters) > 1 and (hits[0] + n) - clusters[-1][-1] <= window:\n        clusters[0] = clusters.pop() + clusters[0]\n    out = []\n    for cluster in clusters:\n        peak = max(\n            (j % n for i in cluster for j in range(i, i + window)),\n            key=lambda j: orient * turns[j],\n        )\n        out.append(pts[(peak + 1) % n])\n    return out\n\n\n# Cooling contraction by material, in percent. `warp_area` was calibrated on a PLA\n# plate, so PLA is the unit: a plastic that contracts five times as much peels the same\n# corners off a fifth of the area. The figures are the guides' (Prusa's material pages\n# put ABS at 1-2% shrink and flatly refuse bed-covering ABS, ASA or PC parts; Hubs\n# gives 0.2-1% across materials), rounded to one calibration point per family.\nSHRINK = {\n    \"pla\": 0.3,\n    \"petg\": 0.3,\n    \"abs\": 1.5,\n    \"asa\": 1.5,\n    \"pc\": 2.0,\n    \"pp\": 2.0,\n}\n\n\n@rule(\"warp_risk\")\ndef warp_risk(shape, ctx):\n    \"\"\"A first layer big enough for cooling contraction to peel its corners.\n\n    Every layer shrinks as it cools and pulls toward the middle of the part. On a\n    small part first-layer adhesion wins. On a big flat plate the accumulated pull\n    beats it, and it lets go where the pull concentrates: a sharp plan corner,\n    farthest from the middle and holding on at a point. The design-side fixes are in\n    the outline, which is why this is a CAD finding and elephant's foot is not:\n    round the vertical corners past `warp_radius` so the peel front is a curve, and\n    prefer a ribbed floor to a solid slab, which halves what contracts. The brim is\n    the slicer's share and the message says so, but a brim on sharp corners is\n    treating the symptom.\n\n","total_lines":1668}},"locations":[]}

{"type":"tool_call_update","toolCallId":"call-55f72674-6343-48f3-8ea6-f42c5a94f3c1-28","status":"completed","content":[{"type":"content","content":{"type":"text","text":"1→\"\"\"The polish pass: chamfer as much of a set as the kernel will take.\n\n`chamfer` is all or nothing. One edge that cannot land takes the whole call down, and\nthe natural response is to shrink the set by hand until it builds. That is how a part\nwith ninety exposed edges ends up with three chamfered ones, and it is why the same\ndoctrine produces far more chamfers in a GUI, where a human adds them one feature at a\ntime and works around each collision individually.\n\nThe doctrine describes this algorithm and used to leave every project to write it. It\n10→was 35 lines in one `system.py`, which meant the next project would write it again or,\nfar more likely, skip it and hand-narrow the set, which is exactly what the rule exists\nto prevent.\n\"\"\"\n\nimport collections.abc\nimport functools\n\nfrom build123d import chamfer as _chamfer\n\n20→# What OCCT says when a chamfer will not land. The same strings `nurb verify`\n# matches on, because both are asking the same question: did the kernel refuse, or did\n# the part refuse in its own words.\nKERNEL = (\"Failed creating a chamfer\", \"BRep_API\")\n\n\ndef _advice(count, size, word):\n    \"\"\"What the doctrine knows about this failure, said at the moment it happens.\n\n    The kernel's own message is \"try a smaller length value(s)\", and the doctrine is\n30→    explicit that following it would never have found the real rule: a chamfer fails\n    for room, not for length. Shrinking it is the one response that makes a part quietly\n    worse, because a 0.4mm chamfer lands and then reads as a defect on the print.\n\n    So the rule goes here rather than only in `nurb rules`. This is the most common way\n    a part stops building, and an error is the one place a reader is guaranteed to be\n    looking.\n    \"\"\"\n    lines = [\n        \"\",\n40→        f\"  A {word} fails for room, not for length, and shrinking it is usually the\",\n        f\"  wrong fix. Two {word}ed convex edges need more than {2 * size:g}mm of face between\",\n        f\"  them, and a single one needs more than {size:g}mm.\",\n    ]\n    if count > 1:\n        lines += [\n            \"\",\n            f\"  This call passed {count} edges as one batch, and a batch is all or nothing:\",\n            \"  one edge that cannot land takes the whole call down. Every edge in it very\",\n            \"  likely chamfers fine on its own, so testing them one at a time will report\",\n50→            \"  that nothing is wrong.\",\n            \"\",\n            # `!r` not `:g`: a size is a measurement, and this codebase reads a bare `1`\n            # as a count. Suggested code has to echo back the float the caller passed.\n            f\"  polish(shape, edges, {size!r}) bisects the set for you and keeps the halves that\",\n            \"  build, which is what the doctrine prescribes instead of narrowing by hand.\",\n        ]\n    else:\n        lines += [\n            \"\",\n60→            \"  A single edge that fails at every length is the other case: its end lands on\",\n            \"  a vertex with four faces and only three edges between them, and OCCT has no\",\n            \"  cap for that corner. Chamfer in two passes and reselect from the result.\",\n        ]\n    lines += [\"\", \"  `nurb rules` has both cases in full.\"]\n    return \"\\n\".join(lines)\n\n\ndef _count(objects):\n    try:\n70→        return len(list(objects))\n    except TypeError:  # a single Edge or Vertex, which is not iterable\n        return 1\n\n\ndef _guarded(fn, word, objects, size, *args, **kwargs):\n    # A generator would be exhausted by the failing call, so the count in the message\n    # would read zero and the advice would describe the wrong case. {"type":"tool_call","toolCallId":"call-ee371d72-763c-47b1-bf7f-8ba027feb792-30","title":"write","kind":"write","status":"pending","toolName":"write","rawInput":{"file_path":"parts/pole_rest.py","content":"from nurb import *\n\n# Pole axis is a bench interface: 18 mm above the bed, centered on the rest in X.\nAXIS_HEIGHT = 18.0\n# Soft finish: sit close enough to cradle, far enough not to smear.\nCRADLE_GAP = 0.2\nWALL = 3.0\nLENGTH = 24.0\n\n\n@part\ndef pole_rest(pole_diameter=measured(\"pole_diameter\"), draft=False):\n    \"\"\"Rest that cradles a freshly finished pole while the finish dries.\n\n    pole_diameter: width of the pole this rest holds\n    \"\"\"\n    if pole_diameter < 8.0:\n        reject(\n            f\"pole_diameter {pole_diameter} is too small to cradle; raise it to 8 or more\",\n            param=\"pole_diameter\",\n        )\n\n    inner_r = pole_diameter / 2.0 + CRADLE_GAP\n    floor = AXIS_HEIGHT - inner_r\n    if floor < WALL:\n        reject(\n            f\"pole_diameter {pole_diameter} needs a cradle deeper than the 18 mm axis \"\n            f\"height allows with a {WALL:g} mm floor; use a smaller pole\",\n            param=\"pole_diameter\",\n        )\n\n    width = 2.0 * (inner_r + WALL)\n\n    with BuildPart() as built:\n        with BuildSketch(Plane.XZ):\n            Rectangle(width, AXIS_HEIGHT, align=(Align.CENTER, Align.MIN))\n            with Locations((0, AXIS_HEIGHT)):\n                Circle(inner_r, mode=Mode.SUBTRACT)\n        extrude(amount=LENGTH / 2.0, both=True)\n\n    body = built.part\n    if draft:\n        return body\n\n    bed = body.bounding_box().min.Z\n    keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z > bed + 1e-4)\n    keep = keep.filter_by(lambda e: e not in set(concave_edges(body)))\n    return polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n"},"content":[],"locations":[]}

{"type":"tool_call","toolCallId":"call-ee371d72-763c-47b1-bf7f-8ba027feb792-31","title":"write","kind":"write","status":"pending","toolName":"write","rawInput":{"file_path":"parts/pole_rest.md","content":"# pole_rest\n\nA bench rest for a freshly finished pole. Several sit in a row; the pole lies\nalong Y across them while the finish dries.\n\n## What it is\n\nA short U-block with a cylindrical cradle. The pole drops in from above and\nsits in a seat just larger than itself, so the finish rests on a surface rather\nthan on edges.\n\n## Design notes\n\n- Axis is fixed at Z=18 mm, centered on the footprint in X, regardless of pole size.\n- Cradle radius is `pole_diameter / 2 + 0.2 mm`: 0.1 mm of clearance, still within\n  0.4 mm of the pole so the contact is a 180° arc, not two lines.\n- 3 mm of wall beside and below the seat. Jaws stop at the equator so the pole\n  lowers straight down.\n- Prints in the use pose, trough open to +Z.\n\n## Don't\n\n- Don't wrap past 180°. A deeper C blocks drop-in.\n- Don't use a V-block. Line contact is not a 120° cradle and will mark a soft finish.\n- Don't let the cradle gap grow past 0.4 mm or shrink under 0.1 mm.\n\n## Changelog\n\n- Initial U-cradle sized from `pole_diameter`, axis locked at 18 mm.\n"},"content":[],"locations":[]}

Several sit in a row; the pole lies\nalong Y across them while the finish dries.\n\n## What it is\n\nA short U-block with a cylindrical cradle. The pole drops in from above and\nsits in a seat just larger than itself, so the finish rests on a surface rather\nthan on edges.\n\n## Design notes\n\n- Axis is fixed at Z=18 mm, centered on the footprint in X, regardless of pole size.\n- Cradle radius is `pole_diameter / 2 + 0.2 mm`: 0.1 mm of clearance, still within\n  0.4 mm of the pole so the contact is a 180° arc, not two lines.\n- 3 mm of wall beside and below the seat. Jaws stop at the equator so the pole\n  lowers straight down.\n- Prints in the use pose, trough open to +Z.\n\n## Don't\n\n- Don't wrap past 180°. A deeper C blocks drop-in.\n- Don't use a V-block. Line contact is not a 120° cradle and will mark a soft finish.\n- Don't let the cradle gap grow past 0.4 mm or shrink under 0.1 mm.\n\n## Changelog\n\n- Initial U-cradle sized from `pole_diameter`, axis locked at 18 mm.\n","_meta":{"details":[{"old_string":"# pole_rest\n\n## What it is\n\n## Design notes\n\n## Don't\n\n## Changelog\n","old_line":1,"new_string":"# pole_rest\n\nA bench rest for a freshly finished pole. What was missing is any reason to type `nurb` at\n50→    all. bb.min.Y) + 4\n    pole = Cylinder(r, L)\n    pole = pole.rotate(Axis.X, 90).move(Location((cx, 0, axis_z)))\n    # 0.1 clearance zone\n    tight = Cylinder(r + 0.1, L).rotate(Axis.X, 90).move(Location((cx, 0, axis_z)))\n    inter = shape.intersect(tight)\n    iv = inter.volume if inter is not None else 0.0\n    print(f\"intersect r+0.1 volume: {iv:.6f}\")\n\n    # drop-in slab: |X-cx| <= r+0.1, Z >= axis_z, Y covering part\n    slab_w = 2 * (r + 0.1)\n    slab_h = 40\n    slab = Box(slab_w, L, slab_h, align=(Align.CENTER, Align.CENTER, Align.MIN)).move(Location((cx, 0, axis_z)))\n    inter2 = shape.intersect(slab)\n    iv2 = inter2.volume if inter2 is not None else 0.0\n    print(f\"intersect drop-in slab volume: {iv2:.6f}\")\n\n    # Sample contact arc at Y=0\n    def in_part(p):\n        # is_inside can be picky; use distance\n        v = Vertex(*p)\n        try:\n            dist = shape.distance_to(v)\n            # distance_to returns (distance, point on shape) or a float?\n            if isinstance(dist, tuple):\n                dist = dist[0]\n            return dist\n        except Exception as e:\n            return f\"err {e}\"\n\n    # Check radial distances from axis\n    ys = [0.0, 0.3 * (bb.max.Y), -0.3 * (bb.max.Y), 0.4 * (bb.max.Y)]\n    for y in ys:\n        hits = []\n        for deg in range(-90, 91, 2):\n            a = math.radians(deg)  # 0 = +X, but we want 0 = down\n            # theta=0 at bottom: X = r sin, Z = axis - r cos\n            th = math.radians(deg)  # deg from bottom, -90 left equator to +90 right\n            # wait: deg -90 is left, 0 bottom, +90 right\n            # X = (r+gap)*sin(th), Z = axis - (r+gap)*cos(th) with th from -90 to 90, th=0 bottom\n            # at th=0: X=0, Z=axis-r  bottom. at th=90: X=r, Z=axis. Good.\n            for gap, label in [(0.05, \"in\"), (0.2, \"seat\"), (0.4, \"near\"), (1.2, \"back\")]:\n                pass\n            # material within 0.4: some point between gap 0.1 and 0.4 should be in solid\n            found = False\n            backed = False\n            for gap in (0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40):\n                x = cx + (r + gap) * math.sin(th)\n                z = axis_z - (r + gap) * math.cos(th)\n                dist = shape.distance_to(Vertex(x, y, z))\n                if isinstance(dist, tuple):\n                    dist = dist[0]\n                if dist < 0.05:\n                    found = True\n                    # backing: point at gap+1.2\n                    x2 = cx + (r + gap + 1.2) * math.sin(th)\n                    z2 = axis_z - (r + gap + 1.2) * math.cos(th)\n                    dist2 = shape.distance_to(Vertex(x2, y, z2))\n                    if isinstance(dist2, tuple):\n                        dist2 = dist2[0]\n                    backed = dist2 < 0.05\n                    break\n            if found and backed:\n                hits.append(deg)\n        # longest continuous run\n        if not hits:\n            print(f\"  y={y:.2f}: NO CONTACT\")\n            continue\n        hits = sorted(hits)\n        # find longest consecutive (step 2)\n        best = 1\n        run = 1\n        for i in range(1, len(hits)):\n            if hits[i] - hits[i-1] <= 2:\n                run += 1\n                best = max(best, run)\n            else:\n                run = 1\n        arc = (best - 1) * 2  # degrees\n        print(f\"  y={y:.2f}: contact degrees span {hits[0]}..{hits[-1]} n={len(hits)} longest_arc≈{arc}°\")\n\nanalyze(20.0)\nanalyze(18.0)\nanalyze(22.0)\nPY","description":"Mechanically verify fit, drop-in, and cradle arc"},"content":[],"locations":[]}

slab_h = 40\n    slab = Box(slab_w, L, slab_h, align=(Align.CENTER, Align.CENTER, Align.MIN)).move(Location((cx, 0, axis_z)))\n    inter2 = shape.intersect(slab)\n    iv2 = inter2.volume if inter2 is (r + 0.09) * math.cos(th)\n            if inside((x, y, z)):\n                bad_clear += 1\n                if bad_clear <= 3:\n                    print(f\"  CLEARANCE FAIL at deg={deg} y={y:.2f} p=({x:.2f},{y:.2f},{z:.2f})\")\n    print(f\"  clearance fails (r+0.09 inside part): {bad_clear}\")\n\n    ys = [0.0, 0.25*(bb.max.Y), -0.25*(bb.max.Y), 0.4*(bb.max.Y), -0.4*(bb.max.Y)]\n    good_len = 0\n    y_span = bb.max.Y - bb.min.Y\n    for y in ys:\n        hits = []\n        for deg in range(-90, 91, 2):\n            th = math.radians(deg)\n            found = False\n            backed = False\n            for gap in (0.12, 0.16, 0.20, 0.24, 0.28, 0.32, 0.36, 0.40):\n                x = cx + (r + gap) * math.sin(th)\n                z = axis_z -
